strengths: Formulates and addresses a highly realistic and under-explored problem setting that concurrently handles channel dependency, sampling asynchrony (differing sampling periods), and block-wise test-time missingness.

Proposes a well-designed architecture utilizing channel tokens as global anchors and a unified read-only attention masking mechanism, allowing the model to natively process variable-length inputs across channels without requiring interpolation.

Provides a comprehensive evaluation including practical variants of standard benchmarks and a real-world industrial dataset (LNG Cargo Handling System), consistently outperforming strong baselines with clear error bars provided.

Includes a thorough spectral and frequency-domain analysis explaining why standard interpolation degrades forecasting performance and demonstrating how the proposed interpolation-free approach preserves spectral fidelity.
weaknesses: High computational complexity: processing all local and channel tokens jointly in a single unified attention layer scales quadratically with the total number of tokens across all channels, posing scalability challenges for datasets with many channels.

While comparing with standard multivariate forecasting baselines using interpolation is fair, the evaluation would be even stronger if it compared against continuous-time or irregular time series models (e.g., Contiformer, MTANs) that also natively handle asynchronous time steps.
The dominant frequency selection via FFT to determine patch length relies on a single peak, which might be sub-optimal for complex channels with multiple co-existing periodicities.

strengths: Highly Realistic and Important Problem Setting: The paper moves away from idealized assumptions (identical sampling rates, complete data) and targets three critical, co-occurring challenges in real-world time series: asynchronous sampling, block-wise test-time missingness, and inter-channel dependencies.

Elegant and Unified Architecture: ChannelTokenFormer (CTF) handles varying sequence lengths across channels naturally via dynamic patching and a read-only global channel token mechanism. By decoupling local temporal tokens from cross-channel aggregation, it avoids the need for alignment or lossy interpolation.

Rigorous and Comprehensive Evaluation: The model is validated on three modified benchmark datasets and one real-world industrial dataset (LNG Cargo Handling System). The experiments cover asynchronous forecasting, test-time block missingness, and conventional multivariate forecasting, where CTF consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

Deep Analysis and Technical Clarity: The paper is exceptionally well-structured and written. The inclusion of a spectral analysis on why linear interpolation degrades forecasting (Appendix B) adds great theoretical value. The ablation studies on attention masking strategies (CI vs CD, read-only vs mutual) are highly detailed and informative.
weaknesses: Computational and Memory Complexity: Since the model flattens local and global tokens across all channels into a single sequence for unified attention, the attention complexity is quadratic with respect to the total number of tokens ($T = \sum_{i} (L^{(i)} + C)$). For high-dimensional datasets with many channels and long windows, this design may suffer from substantial scalability limits.

Sensitivity to Frequency-based Dynamic Patching: The patch length determination depends heavily on identifying a 'strong dominant frequency' using FFT. In non-stationary or highly noisy time series where dominant frequencies change dynamically over time or are poorly defined, this heuristic might lead to suboptimal or unstable patch sizes. Further discussion on the fallback mechanism or sensitivity analysis of the FFT threshold would strengthen the work.

Baseline Evaluation Discrepancy: Standard baselines are inherently restricted to uniform inputs and thus evaluated on interpolated versions of the datasets. While this highlights the fundamental limitation of existing architectures, the interpolation process itself might introduce artificial patterns that degrade baseline performance, making the comparison slightly less direct.

strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem: real-world time series often exhibit multi-rate sampling (asynchrony) and block-wise missingness.
The concept of utilizing frequency-based dynamic patching via FFT to adaptively set patch lengths is an interesting way to preserve temporal characteristics.
Extensive evaluation on several constructed datasets and one real-world industrial dataset (CHS), with detailed ablation studies on masking strategies.
Well-written and clear explanation of the spectral distortions introduced by interpolation in the appendix.
weaknesses: Lack of Comparison with Irregular/Multi-Rate Baselines: The paper defines a setting with asynchronous sampling periods and missingness, which is essentially a structured irregular/multi-rate multivariate time series problem. However, the experimental evaluation only compares CTF against standard regular time series models (using linear/forward-fill interpolation). It completely misses comparisons with models specifically designed for irregularly sampled, asynchronous, or multi-rate time series, such as mTANs, Raindrop, Contiformer, or other continuous-time models. Comparing only against interpolated standard models creates an unfair advantage and does not establish whether the proposed method outperforms existing specialized solutions.

Limited Novelty: The core architectural components—namely, channel-specific summary tokens acting as bottlenecks/attention anchors, read-only masking strategies, and FFT-based patching—are heavily borrowed from existing literature (e.g., read-only prompt attention, TimesNet's FFT period detection, and various Transformer bottleneck/global-token methods). The integration of these components is engineering-heavy but lacks a fundamental theoretical or methodological breakthrough.

Information Bottleneck in Decoding: Only the global channel tokens (C tokens, where C is typically 1 or 2 as shown in Table 4) are passed to the decoder to generate predictions. Forcing the model to compress the entire temporal history of a channel into a tiny number of tokens represents an extreme information bottleneck. This likely explains the amplitude attenuation and over-smoothing issues discussed in Section G. Standard forecasting models retain local patch resolutions for decoding, which is crucial for capturing high-frequency transitions.

Marginal Improvements on Baseline Performance: In Table 1, the performance improvement of CTF over some of the baseline models (which are heavily handicapped by having to use interpolation) is relatively small. For instance, on ETT1, CTF achieves 0.398 CMSE, while PatchTST (which treats channels independently and uses basic interpolation) achieves 0.414. In the conventional setting (Table 11), CTF does not consistently outperform state-of-the-art models like SimpleTM or iTransformer, and in some cases (such as ETTh2), it performs visibly worse.

Practical Sensitivity of FFT-based Patching: The patch length is determined dynamically using the dominant frequency from the FFT of the input sequence. In practice, real-world time series inputs are often noisy, and the dominant frequency can shift dynamically across different sliding windows. The paper does not analyze the stability of this dynamic patching mechanism or how noise in the input window affects the patch length determination and subsequent forecasting performance.

strengths: Addresses a highly realistic and practical forecasting setting involving channel-wise asynchronous sampling, block-wise missingness, and cross-channel dependencies simultaneously, whereas prior works usually study these in isolation.

Provides a strong theoretical and empirical analysis of the spectral distortions (amplitude attenuation, phase delay, etc.) introduced by standard linear interpolation preprocessing, motivating the need for interpolation-free models.

The proposed ChannelTokenFormer uses an elegant unified attention mask with read-only/mutual channel tokens that act as global anchors, enabling the integration of variable-length local patches from different channels.

Extensive and rigorous experimental evaluation across five adapted benchmark datasets and one real-world industrial dataset (CHS), comparing against a diverse range of state-of-the-art baselines (channel-dependent, channel-independent, and irregular models) and showing consistent performance improvements.

The paper is exceptionally well-written, with highly informative figures, detailed appendix sections, extensive ablation studies (including 6 attention masking variants), and scalability/robustness analyses.
weaknesses: Scalability is a bottleneck: since all local and channel tokens are processed in a unified attention layer, the complexity is quadratic in the total number of tokens. Table 12 shows that the model hits an Out-of-Memory (OOM) error at 280 channels on a 24GB GPU, which may limit its applicability in very high-dimensional industrial settings.

The dynamic patching relies on estimating a static dominant frequency via FFT on each input channel. If the time series is highly non-stationary or has time-varying frequencies, a single static dominant period might not be optimal, which is not thoroughly discussed.

The description of the decoder stage in the main text (how the compressed channel tokens are mapped back to the target horizons $Hi$) is quite brief and would benefit from more formal mathematical formulation.

strengths: Practical and highly realistic problem formulation: The paper targets three key challenges of real-world multivariate time series forecasting simultaneously—channel-wise asynchronous sampling, test-time block-wise missingness, and cross-channel dependencies—which are often ignored or oversimplified by existing approaches.

Well-designed and elegant architecture: The proposed ChannelTokenFormer (CTF) utilizes a frequency-based dynamic patching scheme to handle varying temporal resolutions and introduces a read-only mask-guided attention mechanism. This design elegantly separates intra-channel temporal modeling from inter-channel dependency modeling via global channel tokens, avoiding costly patch-to-patch cross-channel interactions.

Extensive and thorough experimental evaluation: The authors adapted several standard benchmarks to realistic asynchronous and missingness settings (ETT-practical, Weather-practical, Monash-SolarWind-practical, EPA-Air) and evaluated on a private real-world LNG industrial dataset. CTF consistently outperforms a wide range of state-of-the-art baselines.

Comprehensive analytical depth: The paper provides excellent additional analyses, including a rigorous frequency bias analysis (explaining and visualizing how interpolation distorts spectral properties and how CTF avoids this), detailed ablation studies on each component, parameter sensitivity analysis on channel tokens, and empirical scalability tests.
weaknesses: Computational complexity and physical scalability: Although the mask-guided attention restricts token interaction conceptually, if implemented using standard dense attention with a masking matrix, the physical memory and computational complexity remain quadratic, $O(T^2)$, where $T = \sum_{i=1}^N (L_i + C)$. This is reflected in the scalability analysis where the model hits Out-Of-Memory (OOM) at 280 channels on a 24GB GPU. It would be helpful to clarify if the authors leveraged block-sparse attention kernels (e.g., FlashAttention) to physically bypass the quadratic overhead of masked regions.

Potential limitations of FFT-based patching: The dynamic patching relies on identifying a dominant frequency via FFT. In highly non-stationary or noisy time series (e.g., financial data or highly irregular industrial signals), a distinct dominant peak may not exist. While a 'sampling-aware fallback' is briefly mentioned, more details on the fallback's design and how often it was triggered across the evaluated datasets would strengthen the paper.

Absence of a strong two-stage baseline (Advanced Imputation + Forecaster): For the missingness evaluation, baseline models are compared using simple linear interpolation or zero-filling. Comparing against a robust two-stage pipeline—where a state-of-the-art imputation method (e.g., SAITS or BRITS) is first applied to handle missingness, followed by a strong forecaster (e.g., PatchTST)—would offer a more complete picture of the benefits of CTF's end-to-end design.

strengths: Realistic and practical problem formulation addressing three simultaneous challenges of real-world multivariate time series: channel-wise sampling asynchrony, block-wise missingness, and complex channel dependencies.

Elegant technical design using a unified mask-guided self-attention mechanism. It manages both intra-channel temporal modeling and inter-channel interactions in a single step using read-only global channel tokens.
Avoids interpolation-induced spectral distortion (such as phase delays and amplitude attenuation) by operating directly on the original observed values with frequency-based adaptive patching.

Comprehensive and thorough empirical evaluation on both adapted standard benchmarks (ETT, Weather, SolarWind) and real-world datasets with inherent irregularity (EPA-Air, LNG Cargo Handling System), showing clear superiority over a massive set of diverse baselines.
weaknesses: Scalability limitations: Since the unified sequence length scales with both local patches and global channel tokens, the quadratic complexity over channel counts leads to out-of-memory (OOM) issues at around 280 channels on a 24GB GPU. This restricts applicability to large-scale industrial systems with thousands of sensors.

Sensitivity of frequency-based dynamic patching: The performance depends on identifying clear periodicities via FFT. For highly non-stationary, noisy, or chaotic sequences where dominant frequencies are absent or shift over time, the fallback patching scheme is triggered, which may reduce the benefits of the frequency-aware design.

Lack of detail on metric scale-normalization: The paper defines Channel-aggregated MSE (CMSE) as the primary evaluation metric. It is unclear if there is any channel-wise scale normalization (like RevIN) applied to prevent channels with larger absolute scales/variances from dominating the overall average metric value.
